nameStory: This plant gets its 'bird's-foot' name from its seed pods, which split into several narrow segments that spread out like the toes of a bird's foot. The 'trefoil' part refers to its three-leaflet leaves (though it actually has five leaflets total - three main ones plus two smaller ones at the base). It's called 'greater' because it's noticeably larger than its common cousin, the regular bird's-foot trefoil.
description: Greater bird's-foot trefoil is a knee-high wildflower in the pea family that loves wet, marshy spots. This herbaceous perennial grows 8-30 inches tall with clusters of bright golden-yellow flowers that look like tiny pea blossoms. Each leaf is made up of five oval leaflets, and the whole plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit. It's much larger and more robust than the common bird's-foot trefoil you might see in drier areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of 5-12 bright golden-yellow pea-like flowers at stem tips, each flower about half an inch long with the classic butterfly shape of legume flowers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Always hollow stems that feel soft and squishy when gently pinched - this is the key difference from other bird's-foot trefoils

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Five-leaflet leaves with three larger oval leaflets at the tip (each about an inch long) and two smaller ones at the base where the leaf meets the stem

idTips.label: Flower Buds
idTips.description: Distinctive green star pattern formed by the sepal tips that curve backward at the ends of unopened flower buds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Larger and more upright than common bird's-foot trefoil, often forming patches in wet areas with stems reaching waist-high

habitat: Look for greater bird's-foot trefoil in consistently moist, open areas like wet meadows, marsh edges, ditches, and poorly drained fields. It thrives in neutral soils that stay damp through the growing season, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. Unlike its drier-habitat relatives, this species needs wet feet to flourish.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the base with fresh five-leaflet leaves appearing as the weather warms. Plants begin developing their characteristic hollow stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright golden flower clusters most abundant in June and July. The distinctive hollow stems are most obvious during active growth.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods develop, splitting into the characteristic bird's-foot shape. Leaves may begin to yellow as growth slows.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground as a perennial, with only dried stems and seed pods remaining visible above ground until snow cover.

funFact: This plant is actually a matchmaker for one of Europe's most delicate butterflies - the wood white butterfly specifically seeks out greater bird's-foot trefoil to lay its eggs on, making the plant an essential nursery for the next generation of these graceful insects.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with regular bird's-foot trefoil, but the hollow stems are the dead giveaway - gently squeeze the stem and if it feels soft and squishy like a drinking straw, you've found the greater species. Regular bird's-foot trefoil has solid, firm stems and grows in much drier places.
contextualKnowledge: Though native to Europe, this plant has been introduced to parts of North America where it's sometimes considered a weedy species in irrigated areas. In New England, it's quite rare with only 10 recorded observations, making it an exciting find for plant enthusiasts.
compareHints: Greater bird's-foot trefoil is the giant of the bird's-foot trefoil family, significantly larger and more robust than both regular bird's-foot trefoil and narrow-leaf bird's-foot trefoil. While its cousins prefer dry, sunny spots and have solid stems, this species loves wet feet and always has those telltale hollow, squishy stems. The flower clusters are also notably larger with more individual blooms per cluster.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bird's-foot trefoil is much more common than its relatives narrow-leaf bird's-foot trefoil and greater bird's-foot trefoil in New England.
Compared to regular bird's-foot trefoil, this species is much more delicate with narrower leaves, thinner stems, and smaller flowers.
